sections.title: be- doesn't always mean 'into'
sections.content: You already know befejezni as a fixed phrase from talking about your evening — now look at its parts. be- glues onto fejez ('to complete a stage of something') to give befejez, 'to finish'. Here be- isn't pointing you into a place the way it did in bemegy; Hungarian prefixes often carry this second, more abstract job of marking an action as wrapped up and complete. Because you almost always finish one specific, particular thing, befejez usually takes a definite object — and the definite conjugation that goes with it.

items.english: I finish the report before five.

items.spanish: Károly befejezi a munkát, és hazamegy.
items.english: Károly finishes work, and goes home.

items.spanish: Reggel elindulok, kilenckor elkezdek dolgozni, és ötkor befejezem a munkát.
items.english: In the morning I set off, at nine I start working, and at five I finish work.

sections.content: Notice the object pattern: elkezdek dolgozni uses a bare infinitive with no specific thing named, so it takes the plain -ek ending. befejezem a munkát names the definite thing being finished — a munkát, 'the work' — so befejez takes the -em/-ed/-i definite endings you already met with verbs like szeret and ért. A definite, specific object usually calls for the definite conjugation, whichever verb you're using.
